docs.motion.component: **Motion** is how game-kit gets a node from one resting pose to the next — by easing it there, not teleporting it. A move, a deal, a card flying home from an illegal drop: the tree changes, and the view catches up over the one clock.
## Identity, not a diff

A settle is not a comparison of two trees. Each node keeps its identity across the change, and its spring plays from where it is to where it now belongs. The runtime holds the one clock — a node never starts its own ticker — and animates only while something is in flight, then stops.
## Gesture vs settle

While a finger owns a node it tracks the finger one-to-one; it does not ease. The settle is what happens after — the card let go, the run dropped, the stock dealt. That split is why a drag feels direct and a release feels smooth. Flip these controls to watch a settle on its own, with no drag involved.
## The tuning — one flat record, every number of feel

Every number that decides how a motion feels is a field of `MotionTuning`, and this page is that record, field by field: each control below is the field it is named after, handed to the clock as it stands. Three levels stack — the kit's defaults, the game's own record (`attachMotion(host, painter, { settleMs: 240 })`), a per-call patch (`grab(items, { anchor, lift: 1 })`) — and above them the **viewer's speed** (the header's ▶ ladder, `ViewerSettings.motionSpeed`: `0` is no animation, `1` the designer's timing, `2` twice as fast) multiplies everything for this onlooker only.
| field | default | what it decides |
| `settleMs` · `settleEase` | 180 · `easeOut` | the glide of a node to a moved seat |
| `flipMs` · `flipEase` | 180 · `linear` | the squeeze to an edge and back of a turn-over |
| `shuffleMs` | 700 | the length of a shuffle's choreography |
| `rollMs` | 900 | the length of a die's tumble |
| `carry` · `lift` | `rigid` · 1.06 | how a run composes under the finger; the pop while held |
| `followStiffness` · `followDamping` | 120 · 14 | the chase spring — the lag behind the finger and its settle |
| `liftStiffness` · `liftDamping` | 170 · 20 | how fast the pop arrives |
| `leanFactor` · `leanMaxDeg` | 6.42 · 17.19 | how far a run banks into speed, and where it saturates |
| `leanStiffness` · `leanDamping` | 150 · 16 | the bank's own spring: a hand that turns round swings the lean across in the spring's time, it does not jump |
| `gravity` · `bounce` | 9 · 0.7 | a throw down the screen: the pull, the floor's give |
| `glide` · `spinGlide` | normal · normal | a throw across the desk: the run-out law for the speed and for the turn |
A running clock retunes live (`motions.retune(patch)`) — a designer's settings screen changes numbers on the standing desk, and so does every slider here.
docs.motion.settle: One token, two slots. Toggle the control and the node eases from the left seat to the right and back — the same glide a card makes settling into a pile, driven here by a control instead of a hand.
docs.motion.deal: A stacked pack fans into a row on deal. Every card keeps its identity across the change, so each one springs from the stack to its own seat rather than the picture being redrawn in place.
docs.motion.flip: One card turned over on the clock. `turned` is the trigger — flip it and the clock plays a turn: the card squeezes to an edge, the side swaps THERE (where it has no width to show the swap), and it grows back on the far side. `flipMs` and `flipEase` are the turn's own numbers, apart from the settle's; `linear` is a physical rotation, `easeOut` a snappier turn.
docs.motion.carry:
A column under your own finger, every number of the carry on one panel. Grab any card and it leads the run below it. `followStiffness`/`followDamping` are the chase spring — the LAG behind your pointer and how it settles; `lift`/`liftStiffness`/`liftDamping` the pop; `leanFactor`/`leanMaxDeg` how the run banks into speed, `leanStiffness`/`leanDamping` the spring that bank rides (turn your finger round mid-drag: the swing has weight instead of snapping); `carry` how it composes (`rigid` — one plank about the grab, `loose` — each card about its own middle). Let go: nothing here accepts a drop, so the run flies home on `settleMs`/`settleEase`.

AND THE TRAY IS REAL WHILE THE RUN IS IN HAND. Carried into a border it stops there and goes on straining after the finger; shove it in at `wallSpeed` or more and the wall wins — the run comes off the hand and slides back with `wallBounce` of the speed it arrived at; keep pulling past `leash` and the hold breaks, leaving the run standing on the wall. What flies back is the game's word: this stand answers with a plain slide, while a die (`Add-ons/Dice` · Throw) throws itself and tumbles.
docs.motion.launch: A throw DOWN THE SCREEN. `launched` is the trigger: the card leaves with `speed` along `angle` (270 is straight up), `gravity` pulls it, the bottom edge of the glass gives it back by `bounce`, it spins at `spin`, and once it is off the glass it eases home. `retain` keeps every frame on the glass and paints only what flies — the trail of the old solitaire's victory cascade, which is exactly this call, once per card, with a stagger.
docs.motion.slide: A throw ACROSS THE DESK, seen from above: no gravity — `glide` bleeds the speed and `spinGlide` the spin, the tray's walls reflect by `bounce`, and where it stops it stops. This scene writes nothing into the tree, so it then eases home; a die's throw is exactly this with the landing written and a face shown (`Add-ons/Dice`).
docs.motion.shuffle: A row reordered on the clock — three layers a game keeps apart. `seed` decides the ORDER: `permutation(n, seededRng(seed))`, the same on every client that shares the seed (or the server sends the order outright). `reorder` is the TRUTH: the same children in that order, identity kept. `recipe` is the LOOK — `riffle`, `overhand`, `wash`, `shake` — a choreography over the children by index that never sees the seed. Tap any card to shuffle again, or bump `shuffled` on the panel.
docs.motion.roll: A tumble in place — the look of a die rolled without being thrown: `turns` whole turns about its centre and a `hop` (a scale peak) over `rollMs`. TAP THE TOKEN to tumble it again, or bump `rolled`. What it commits is a game's business (here, nothing) — but WHEN is the runtime's, and it is not a phase: a tumbling piece is cued every 60° of turning, and the commit falls on the LAST of those cues, while the piece is still turning. The token has no faces to show, so it takes the cue on its paint instead: the flashing is the cadence, quick at first and thinning out with the turn, and the last one puts the paint back. That is the beat a die's face changes on.
docs.motion.shiver: The tremble that says NOTED, and nothing more. It exists for the moment a long press is recognised: the finger has been down half a second, the gesture has just changed meaning, and nothing on the glass has said so — and a player who gets no answer lifts their finger to check, cancelling the very gesture they were making. It ends exactly where it began, by the shape of the curve rather than by a correction at the end, and it writes nothing: the card is on its seat when it stops, and the shadow never moved.
docs.motion.bounce: The jump that says LOOK AT ME — the flat cousin of a slide's `hop`, and the pair is the point of having both. A hop leaves the DESK, so its shadow falls away and the piece reads as lifted; a bounce stays on the felt and only travels, so the shadow rides along under it the whole way. One says "picked up", the other "look at me", and a game that reached for the wrong one is telling the player something it did not mean. A choreography and not a flight: it ends where it began, and a body under gravity only does that by accident.
docs.motion.registry: A look is not a verb. The kit's verbs are mechanics it knows the meaning of — a turn-over commits a side, a shuffle an order, a throw ends where the physics says — and their list is closed. A look says "over here", "no", "well done", and there can be no closed list of those, because they are the designer's vocabulary and not the engine's. So they are a registry: `registerMotion(name, recipe)` writes one down and `animate(id, name)` plays it, on the same one clock, with the same hold on the node and the same shadow law every verb gets. `yours` on this page is authored from the panel's own numbers as a keyframe table — a pose out, a pause (two keys with the same values), and home — and its ends are pinned to the seat by construction, so however the table is filled in, the card lands where it left.
